cues.say: Dashboards are live charts of your system's health. Alerts watch those numbers, and automatically page the on-call person when one crosses a line.
Think of a car dashboard: gauges you glance at, and warning lights that demand attention.
Without them, your customers find out first. Checkout fails, people give up, and the on-call engineer has no idea.
So what do you chart? Start with the four golden signals. Latency, usually as p95: the time that ninety-five percent of requests beat. Traffic. Errors. And saturation: how full a resource is.
Then add business metrics: orders a minute, held versus paid, stock left. They show what customers are actually getting.
An alert is a rule on one number: above a line, for some time. Say, errors above two percent for two minutes. The duration means a short blip doesn't wake anyone.
And every alert links to a runbook: a written 'if this fires, do this', with an owner.
Good alerts give you three things. You hear about trouble before customers tell you.
You know what's wrong, not just that something is.
And you know what to do, like which switch to flip.
Now game day at the pizza shop. At three forty PM, held orders keep climbing, but paid orders go flat. A held order has a slot reserved, waiting for payment.
If you only watch errors and latency, both look normal. Customers can't pay, and nobody knows.
So you alert on the gap: held minus paid above fifty, for three minutes. It pages the on-call engineer.
The runbook says: check Stripe's status. If it's down, pause orders.
Here's where it sits: every part reports its numbers to one dashboard, and the alerts watch them there.
Two things to know. Too many alerts get ignored, so page only for what needs a person right now.
And every alert needs an owner and a runbook, or the page wakes someone who can't act.
In the interview, say: if errors pass two percent for two minutes, I turn on the waiting room.
